source_text: φησίν, «ἐστὲ ὑπὸ νόμον, ἀλλ' ὑπὸ χάριν»· 27.50 καὶ αὖθις· «ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ εὐδόκησε πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα κατοικῆσαι καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ ἀποκαταλ λάξαι τὰ πάντα εἰς αὐτόν». 27.51 Ἑπόμενα καὶ ταῦτα τοῖς πρόσθεν. τοῦ γὰρ πατρὸς ἐν τῷ υἱῷ καὶ αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ τῇ φύσει τυγχάνοντος, ὡς καὶ πᾶν συγγενὲς ἀχώριστόν πως τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ συγγενοῦς καθέστηκεν, κἂν τῇ ὑποστάσει διέζευκται, καλὸς καὶ ὁ ἐν τῷ κινουμένῳ ἐδαφίῳ λόγος, εἰ καὶ μὴ ἄγαν βαθέως, ἀλλ' οὐ πᾶσιν εὐσυνόπτως· «δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἀποκαταλλάσσειν τὰ πάντα», ὡς ἁρμόττειν τῷ υἱῷ καὶ τὸ περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς χρησθέν· «ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα», εἴπερ ὑγιῶς ἔχει τά τε νῦν εἰρημένα τό τε· «ἐν αὐτῷ κατοικεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος». 27.52 Καὶ Τιμοθέῳ δὲ γράψας εἰς ἄκρον ἐθεολόγησεν περὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπ' ἀμφοῖν τῶν λέξεων τὸ μὴ εἶναι κατὰ θεότητα παρὰ φύσιν τὴν πατρικὴν ἐδίδαξεν. 27.53 εἶπεν γὰρ τοιῶσδε· «ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐστὶν τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον· θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί, ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι, ὤφθη ἀγγέλοις, ἐκηρύχθη ἔθνεσιν, ἐπιστεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ, ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ». 27.54 οὔπω γὰρ πᾶσιν σαφῶς ἔκδηλος ὢν οὗτος ὁ πάντων γενεσιουργὸς καὶ εὐεργέτης ἐκφανὴς εὑρέθη, ἡνίκα διὰ τὴν πάντων σωτηρίαν ἐγένετο ἐθελοντὴς καὶ ὡς εἷς τῶν πάντων. 27.55 Ὅθεν «ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι», τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἀπεφάνθη ἢτ' οὖν ἐβεβαιώθη καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἀγνοησάντων αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ὄπισθεν χρόνῳ ἀληθινὸς εἶναι θεός· καὶ τοῦτο, φησίν, οὐκ ἀβασανίστως, ἀλλ' αὐτῇ τῇ ψυχικῇ ἡμῶν κινήσει, ὡς ἡ κοινὴ συνήθεια ἔχει λέγειν· "4ὁ δεῖνα ἐδικαιώθη ἀληθινὸς εἶναι υἱὸς τοῦδε"5, πίστιν γένους παρασχόμενος· καὶ ἄλλοτε· "4ὁ δεῖνα ἐδικαιώθη καλῶς ἡγεμονεύειν"5. 27.56 Καὶ ἵνα πιστικώτερος ὁ λόγος φανῇ, ὦφθαι αὐτὸν ἀξιοῖ καὶ ἀγγέλοις, οἷστισι διὰ τὴν θείαν αὐτοῦ ἀπειρίαν καὶ ἀνειδεότητα ἀόρατος ἦν πρὸ ἐκείνου τοῦ χρόνου, ὁμοίως τῷ «μόνῳ ἀοράτῳ θεῷ», καὶ ὑπ' αὐτῶν ὑμνῆσθαι· «δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία»· κεκηρύχθαι δὲ ἐν τῷδε τῷ παντὶ καὶ πεπιστεῦσθαι, ὅτιπερ ὁ ἐκ τοῦ ἀρρήτου φωτὸς ἀχρόνως ἐκλάμψας, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀειπαρθένου ἐν 32 ὑστέροις καιροῖς διὰ φιλανθρωπίαν ἀφράστως ἐτέχθη, τὰ πατρικὰ πάντα ἐκφήνας ἐν ἑαυτῷ· ἀναβεβηκέναι τε πρὸς τὸν πάντα περιειληφότα ἐν δόξῃ, ᾗ ἀεὶ ἐτύγχανεν ὢν μετὰ τοῦ θεοῦ. 27.57 Ἀξιόπιστος δὲ καὶ αὐτός, περὶ οὗ ὁ λόγος, τῇ ἰδίᾳ μαρτυρῶν θεότητι καὶ κυριότητι καὶ λέγων παρὰ Ματθαίῳ μὲν πρὸς τὸν διάβολον· «οὐ μὴ πειράσῃς κύριον τὸν θεόν σου», παρὰ Ἰωάννῃ πρὸς τοὺς ἀποστόλους· «ὑμεῖς φωνεῖτε με· ὁ κύριος καὶ ὁ διδάσκαλος· καὶ καλῶς λέγετε· εἰμὶ γάρ». 27.58 Θωμᾶς δὲ καὶ τύπους ἥλων, οὓς ἔσχεν δι' ἡμᾶς παρ' ἡμῶν ὁ σωτὴρ ὡς φιλάνθρωπος, ψηλαφήσας οὐκ ἐταράχθη οὐδὲ καθυφῆκεν τῆς περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀνωτάτω δόξης· 27.59 ἠπίστατο γάρ, ὡς μόνης τῆς αὐτοκρατορικῆς ἀπειροδυνάμου καὶ ἀγαθωτάτης φύσεως ἦν, οὐ μὴν δὲ κτιστῆς, τὸ μόνον οὐχ ὑπὲρ ἰδίων κτισμάτων παθεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθολικὴν ἥν φαμεν καὶ γενικὴν σωτηρίαν, καὶ ταύτην αἰωνίως, δωρήσασθαι. 27.60 τοιγάρτοι κἀντεῦθεν μᾶλλον ἐπιθαρσήσας ἀντεισφέρει αὐτῷ τὴν βεβαίαν πίστιν καὶ ἀνευφημεῖ· «ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου». 27.61 Καὶ ἐν ταῖς καθολικαῖς δὲ ἐπιστολαῖς ἐξ ἴσου καὶ ὁμοιολέκτως τὸν υἱὸν τῷ πατρὶ θεολογοῦντες ἔγραψαν, ὡς προελέχθη, Ἰωάννης μὲν ὁ πολὺς ἐν θεολόγοις· «καὶ οἴδαμεν», φησίν, «ὅτι ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ἥκει καὶ ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν διάνοιαν, ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινὸν θεόν· καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ, τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνιος». 27.62 ἄλλον, φησίν, μὴ ζήτει τῇ οὐσίᾳ θεὸν ἢ υἱὸν θεοῦ. 27.63 δὶς γὰρ εἶπόν σοι ἐπὶ αὐτοῦ τὸ ἀληθινόν, ὅτι τε «υἱὸς ἀληθινὸς» καὶ «θεὸς ἀληθινός», δεδωκὼς διάνοιαν τοῖς λαβεῖν ἀξίοις· ὥστε ἔχειν εἰδέναι ὡς ἀληθῶς γεγέννηται καὶ ἀληθῶς ἐστι τῷ τεκόντι θεῷ ὁμοούσιος. 27.64 Ἰούδας δὲ ὁ εἰς τοὺς δυοκαίδεκα μονοκτήτορα ὡρίσατο αὐτὸν ὡς τὴν ἐπὶ πάντων καὶ διὰ πάντων καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν πατρικὴν διακληρωσάμενον θεότητα, οὑτωσί που τοῖς ἁπανταχοῦ γράψας· «παρεισέδυσαν γάρ τινες ἄνθρωποι πάλαι προγεγραμμένοι εἰς τοῦτο τὸ κρίμα ἀσεβεῖς, τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριν μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν καὶ τὸν μόνον δεσπότην καὶ κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἀρνούμενοι». 27.65 Ἀλλὰ καὶ Πέτρος ὁ ἐν ἀποστόλοις κορυφαῖος ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν φαίνεται εἰπών· «τὸν λόγον, ὃν ἀπέστειλεν τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ, εὐαγγελιζόμενος εἰρήνην διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ· οὗτός ἐστι πάντων
pass_a_gloss: ['For no longer'] he says, 'are you under law, but under grace'; 27.50 and again: 'because in him all the fullness was well pleased to dwell and through him to reconcile all things into him'. 27.51 These things too are following on the things before. For since the Father is in the Son and he in the Father by nature, as every kindred thing stands somehow unseparated from its own kindred, even if it is disjoined in hypostasis, fine also is the saying in the passage being discussed, even if not very deeply, but not easily surveyed by all: 'through him and into him to reconcile all things', so that there fits the Son also what was uttered about the Father: 'from whom all things', if indeed the things now said hold soundly and the: 'in him dwells all the fullness of the deity'. 27.52 And having written to Timothy he spoke of him as God to the highest point and from both the expressions taught that he is not, according to deity, beside the Father's nature. 27.53 For he spoke in such a way: 'confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: God was made manifest in flesh, was justified in spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory'. 27.54 For not yet being clearly evident to all, this generator and benefactor of all was found manifest, when for the salvation of all he came to be a volunteer and as one of all. 27.55 Whence 'he was justified in spirit', that is, he was declared, or rather confirmed, also by those who did not know him in the time behind, to be true God; and this, he says, not without testing, but by the very soul-movement of ours, as the common usage has it to say: 'so-and-so was justified to be true son of such a one', having furnished proof of birth; and at another time: 'so-and-so was justified to govern well'. 27.56 And so that the account might appear more persuasive, he deems him to have been seen also by angels, to whom on account of his divine boundlessness and formlessness he was invisible before that time, like the 'only invisible God', and to have been hymned by them: 'glory in the highest to God and upon earth peace, among men good pleasure'; and to have been proclaimed in this whole and to have been believed, since the one who shone out timelessly from the unspeakable light, from the ever-virgin in later times through love of man was inexpressibly born, having shown forth all the Father's things in himself; and to have gone up toward the one who has encompassed all, in glory, in which he always happened to be with God. 27.57 And worthy of belief is he himself also, about whom the account is, witnessing to his own deity and lordship and saying in Matthew to the devil: 'you shall not tempt the Lord your God', in John to the apostles: 'you call me: the Lord and the teacher; and you say well; for I am'. 27.58 And Thomas, having touched also the marks of the nails, which the Saviour as man-loving had on account of us from us, was not troubled, nor did he slacken from the highest opinion about him; 27.59 for he understood that it belonged to the only sovereign, boundless-in-power and most good nature, but not indeed to a created one, not only to suffer on behalf of its own creatures, but also to give the salvation which we call universal and general, and this eternally. 27.60 Therefore from this too having taken more courage he brings in return to him the firm faith and hails: 'my Lord and my God'. 27.61 And in the catholic letters, speaking of the Son as God equally and in like words to the Father, they wrote, as was said before, John, the great among theologians: 'and we know', he says, 'that the Word of God has come and gave us understanding, so that we may know the true God; and we are in the true one, the Son of God Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life'. 27.62 Do not seek, he says, a God other in being than the Son of God. 27.63 For twice I told you the 'true' about him, both that 'true Son' and 'true God', having given understanding to those worthy to receive; so as to be able to know that he was truly begotten and truly is same-in-being with the God who bore him. 27.64 And Jude, the one among the twelve, defined him sole-owner as having been allotted the Father's deity over all and through all and in all, writing somewhere thus to those everywhere: 'for some men slipped in, long ago written beforehand for this judgment, ungodly, changing the grace of our God into wantonness and denying the only master and Lord Jesus Christ'. 27.65 But also Peter, the head among apostles, appears in the Acts saying: 'the word which he sent to the sons of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ; this one is of all [...]
pass_b_english: … he says, “are you under law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14). And again: “For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to him” (Colossians 1:19-20).

This too follows from what went before. For the Father is by nature in the Son, and the Son in the Father, just as everything akin stands, in a way, inseparable from what is akin to it, even if it is divided in hypostasis. So the saying in the passage under discussion is fine as well, though it is not very deep, yet not easy for everyone to take in at a glance: “through him and to him to reconcile all things.” Thus the word spoken of the Father, “from whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6), fits the Son too, if indeed both what has now been said and the words “in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead” (Colossians 2:9) hold sound.

Writing to Timothy as well, Paul spoke of him as God in the highest degree, and from both expressions he taught that in his Godhead he is not outside the Father’s nature. For he spoke thus: “Confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). For this Maker and Benefactor of all, who was not yet plainly manifest to all, was found manifest when, for the salvation of all, he willingly became as one of all.

Hence “he was justified in the Spirit”: that is, he was declared, or rather confirmed, to be true God even by those who had not known him in the time before. And this, he says, was not without testing, but by the very movement of our soul, as common usage puts it: “So-and-so was justified as truly the son of such a one,” when he has furnished proof of his descent; and again, “So-and-so was justified in governing well.”

And so that the account may seem more persuasive, he holds that he was seen by angels too, to whom, because of his divine infinity and formlessness, he had been invisible before that time, like “the only invisible God” (1 Timothy 1:17); and that he was hymned by them: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men” (Luke 2:14). He holds that he was preached and believed on in this whole world, because he who shone forth timelessly from the ineffable light was ineffably born of the ever-virgin in later times, out of love for mankind, and showed forth in himself all that is the Father’s; and that he went up to the One who embraces all things, in the glory in which he always was with God.

Worthy of belief, too, is the very one of whom we speak, when he bears witness to his own Godhead and lordship. In Matthew he says to the devil, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 4:7); in John he says to the apostles, “You call me the Lord and the Teacher, and you say well, for so I am” (John 13:13). And Thomas, when he touched the marks of the nails, which the Saviour in his love for mankind bore from us for our sake, was not troubled, nor did he lower his supreme estimate of him. For he knew that it belonged only to the sovereign nature, infinite in power and supremely good, and certainly not to a created one, not only to suffer for its own creatures, but also to bestow the salvation we call universal and general, and that for ever. Therefore, taking still greater courage from this, he offers him firm faith in return and cries out: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

In the catholic epistles too, as was said before, they wrote of the Son as God equally with the Father and in the same words. John, the great among theologians, says: “And we know that the Word of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God; and we are in the true one, in the Son of God, Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). Do not seek, he means, a God other in substance than the Son of God. For I have twice told you that “true” belongs to him: he is both “true Son” and “true God,” who has given understanding to those worthy to receive it; so that you may know that he was truly begotten and is truly consubstantial with the God who begot him.

Jude, one of the twelve, defined him as sole Owner, as one who has received for his lot the Father’s Godhead, which is over all and through all and in all. He writes somewhere in this way to those everywhere: “For certain men have crept in, who long ago were marked out for this judgment, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into licentiousness and denying the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (Jude 4). And Peter too, the chief among the apostles, is shown in the Acts saying: “The word which he sent to the sons of Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ: he is of all …

choices.issue: Duplicated paragraphs, stray line, calque, garbled clauses, abbreviated references
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English gave 27.54-27.56 twice: once in a short draft (p3-p4, which also dropped 'in glory' and the angels' 'seeing') and again in a fuller draft (p6-p7), with the stray line 'speaks without profanity' between them. The duplicate and the stray line are removed; this is why the old English ran to about 1.6 times the Greek. Also fixed: 'the argument on the moving ground' (ἐν τῷ κινουμένῳ ἐδαφίῳ: the passage under discussion), 'he theologized about him to the end' (spoke of him as God in the highest degree), 'if what has been said now and then is held soundly', 'those who had ignored him in later time' (who had not known him in the time before), 'his highest glory' (his supreme estimate of him), 'Seek no other god or Son of God in respect of essence' (a God other in substance than the Son of God), 'who portioned out the paternal divinity' (who has received it for his lot). References: 'Rom 6:14', 'Col 1:19-20', 'Col 2:9', '1 Tim 3:16', 'Matt 4:7' written in full; the second 'Col 1:20' dropped because the clause repeats the verse just cited; 1 Timothy 1:17 added.

ἐδάφιον is a passage of text, κινούμενον 'being discussed'; not 'moving ground'.
Kept as printed; probably 'God' and 'was manifested', the two words Didymus draws on in 27.54.
Read as ἤτοι οὖν; the spacing is the copy-text's.
4 and 5 are footnote markers in the copy-text; skipped. The two sayings are everyday examples of δικαιόω, set as quotations.
32 is a printed page number in the copy-text; debris, skipped.
A word split across printed lines; read whole.
δόξα here is Thomas' opinion of Christ, not glory: he did not lower his belief that Christ is God.
The nominative participle agrees with 'true God', taking up 'has given us understanding' from 1 John 5:20.

choices.english: the Word of God has come
choices.why: Didymus' text of 1 John 5:20 reads 'the Word of God' where the New Testament has 'the Son of God'; translated as he quotes it.
μονοκτήτωρ, a rare compound; Didymus' gloss on Jude's 'only Master' (δεσπότης, owner of slaves).
The section ends mid-quotation (Acts 10:36); the missing word 'Lord' is in the next section and is not supplied here.
